comparator.name: Dutch Language and Culture
comparator.sourceNotes: The current 2026–27 Leiden study product accounts for 180 EC: a 60-EC first-year core, 30 EC of second-year compulsory work, 50 EC of internal specialisation study spanning years two and three, a 10-EC bachelor thesis and 30 EC open elective space. The Dutch Linguistics specialisation group is instantiated because it most directly preserves the programme’s broad Dutch-language identity; its two 10-EC compulsory courses and the first three eligible 10-EC listed choices make the required 50 EC. This choice is made independently of UCR fit. The 0-EC mentoring and thesis-seminar modules are omitted. The 2026–27 programme-specific OER states that formal graduation directions are not applicable, so routeSelection is null even though the study product organises the 50-EC bound-choice space into internal specialisation groups. The fixed-queue reassessment on 2026-10-16 preserves every settled external component and credit weight and the neutral internal Dutch Linguistics choice. The current programme page and 2026–27 OER were rechecked: rhetoric, stylistics, literary interpretation and language/media relations are substantive parts of the target, while formal graduation directions remain inapplicable. Media is integrated into the four disciplinary areas rather than presented as a separate current specialisation.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Nine courses / 67.5 EC differ in each direction. The second programme removes the cognitive/psychological sequence, rhetoric teaching, institutional persuasion and advanced sociological theory. It adds myth and life writing, environmental media/communication, art and museum interpretation, modern/imperial history and local primary-source research. These are curricular consequences of historical literary and cultural interpretation, rather than a relabelled persuasion programme.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two complete and substantively different related programmes are accepted in sequence. A third direction in Dutch structural/historical/social linguistics cannot form a complete 24-course programme: Psycholinguistics addresses acquisition and processing and Style & Meaning addresses textual choices, but neither supplies Dutch phonology, morphology, syntax, historical variation or a sustained sociolinguistics sequence. Introductory Dutch teaches everyday communication rather than academic Dutch analysis. Digital corpora is support-only evidence, not an independently generating direction; a technical data-science programme would add unevidenced priorities, while another media/communication version would repeat the accepted routes. The historical no-match overstated the necessity of full disciplinary equivalence.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both directly teach argumentation and persuasion; the UCR rhetoric foundation is not Dutch-language proficiency study.
Both examine how linguistic choices produce interpretive and rhetorical effects. UCR stylistics does not supply Dutch-specific linguistic progression.
Both concern strategic persuasive communication. UCR directly applies framing and persuasion to institutional communication problems, without reproducing Dutch-specialist study.
Both directly teach literary analysis and interpretation. UCR uses multiple literary traditions rather than a Dutch textual corpus.
Both directly investigate theoretical approaches to interpreting literature. The UCR project is not a Dutch literary-period sequence.

notes.text: Leiden offers a Dutch-language disciplinary curriculum in historical and modern Dutch literature, Dutch structural and social linguistics, rhetoric, media and Dutch Studies research. These UCR programmes pursue related questions through rhetoric, stylistics, literature, media, cognition and cultural history.
